title: Catalan's constant is irrational (proof with the help of AI)
content:
Mathematics > General Mathematics
  [Submitted on 3 Sep 2026]
    Title:Catalan's constant is irrational
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Whether the constant $$G=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(-1)^k}{(2k+1)^2}=\frac1{1^2}-\frac1{3^2}+\frac1{5^2}-\frac1{7^2}+\cdots$$ introduced by Catalan in the nineteen century is irrational, is a long-standing open problem. In this paper we prove the irrationality of $G$ via using suitable weights.

report.summary: A new arXiv paper claims to prove Catalan's constant is irrational, reportedly with AI assistance, resolving a long-standing open problem.
report.background: Catalan's constant G = 1/1² − 1/3² + 1/5² − 1/7² + ... appears in number theory, physics, and combinatorics. Since the 19th century, its irrationality remained open, unlike π and e. Irrationality proofs typically construct rational approximations too good to exist, using continued fractions, Padé approximants, or Apéry-like sums. Apéry's 1978 proof of ζ(3) irrationality sparked interest in odd zeta values, but Catalan's G resisted. Recently, AI systems have begun assisting mathematics by suggesting identities, searching proof strategies, and formalizing results in Lean. The paper's title signals AI was used; the abstract only says the proof uses suitable weights. If correct, it marks a high-profile AI-assisted result in a field where formal verification and peer review are essential.
key_points: The paper claims a proof that G = 1/1² − 1/3² + 1/5² − ... is irrational. This sum, known since the 1800s, was one of the most famous open constants in number theory. The abstract credits suitable weights, suggesting a weighted approximation or integral method, but gives no further technical detail.

The title says with the help of AI, yet the abstract does not describe the AI's role. Possibilities include generating candidate identities, searching proof strategies, or formal verification. Without a methods section, the extent of AI contribution—and whether it is essential or assistive—remains unclear.

If verified, the result would add Catalan's constant to the small set of non-elementary constants proven irrational. It may also validate AI-assisted discovery in mathematics, encouraging similar attacks on other unsolved constants like ζ(5) or the Euler–Mascheroni constant γ.

arXiv papers are not peer-reviewed. The claim needs expert scrutiny and ideally formalization in a proof assistant such as Lean. Irrationality proofs can contain subtle gaps, so independent replication is crucial before treating it as established.
report.impact: For the AI industry, a verified AI-assisted proof would strengthen the case for AI as a mathematical collaborator, not just a calculator. It could accelerate investment in neuro-symbolic systems, proof search, and formal verification. Developers would gain motivation to build tools that combine LLMs with Lean or Coq, improving reliability and explainability. Regular users may not notice immediately, but such results can eventually affect cryptography, algorithm design, and how we trust AI-generated claims. The bigger lesson is verification: AI can propose, but human or machine-checked proof must dispose. Until then, treat the result as a promising preprint, not settled fact.
report.tools: To follow up, watch Lean 4 and mathlib for a possible formalization; Lean Copilot, AlphaProof, and GPT-f for AI proof search; Coq, Isabelle, and HOL Light for independent checking. Connected Papers and alphaXiv can map citations. For the mathematics, read Apéry's proof and surveys on irrationality measures. A public Lean proof would be the strongest signal of correctness.
